source: Time an echo to find a distance: d = vt/2, because the sound goes there and back.
Students forget the sound travels there and back, so their answer is twice the real distance.

Shout toward a cliff and you hear your voice come back: an echo, sound reflected off a surface. If you know the speed of sound and time the echo, you can measure distances you can't reach. Bats, dolphins, ships' sonar and ultrasound scanners all do this.
$$d = \dfrac{v\,t}{2}$$ where $t$ is the time from sending the sound to hearing the echo. Divide by 2 because the sound travels there and back.

In time $t$, the sound covers a total path of $v\,t$. That path goes out to the reflecting surface and returns, so it is twice the distance to the surface. Half of it, $\dfrac{v\,t}{2}$, is the one-way distance.
A pulse travels to the end of a string and reflects back. The round trip covers twice the length of the string.
A ship sends a sound pulse straight down and hears the echo from the seabed 2 s later. Sound travels at 1,500 m/s in seawater. How deep is the sea?
Total path: $1{,}500 \times 2 = 3{,}000$ m, down and back.
You clap and hear the echo from a canyon wall 1.2 s later. Sound travels at 343 m/s. How far away is the wall?

Forgetting that the sound travels there and back, which gives an answer twice the real distance. Check: if your answer is the whole distance the sound traveled in the time, you still need to halve it.
Many bats chirp at frequencies too high for us to hear and judge distances to insects from the echoes, within a fraction of a second.
